newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Astra air cargo volumes to rise in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Astra air cargo volumes to rise in 1997.

text.p: Swedish drug company Astra AB plans to lift its freight volumes to between 4,500 and 5,000 tonnes in 1997 from between 3,500 and 4,000 tonnes this year, a spokesman for Astra's shipping department said on Friday.
"It will be from between 4,500 tonnes up to 5,000 tonnes next year," said Magnus Rehnstrom, shipping manager at Astra.
Shipping volumes would total between 3,500 and 4,000 tonnes this year, calculated by chargeable weight as opposed to actual weight, Rehnstrom told Reuters.
"In the past seven years we have increased the weight 10 times," he said. "At least until the year 2000 it will continue to increase from year to year."
Because Astra's products were lightweight, the company paid by volumes, not weight, Rehnstrom said.
Astra's own staff packed the fragile, temperature-sensitive products into containers.
"We have built up a special system where we pack the airline containers directly on our premises. We send it door-to-door unbroken to our customers," he said.

Astra's main production plant is in Sodertalje, which is outside Stockholm. Most of Astra's products are trucked to Stockholm's international Arlanda airport, Swedish west coast city Gothenburg, Frankfurt or Amsterdam, Rehnstrom said.
Astra's main carriers were Lufthansa, KLM, SAS, Singapore Airlines, Finnair and Air France -- in that order, he said.
Astra was having problems finding freight space to Sydney and sometimes to South America, but he said otherwise capacity was adequate from Sweden.

"We are quite fortunate because we can plan our shipments a couple of weeks before due to the lead times we have in production. Usually we can pre-book two to three weeks before, which makes it possible for us to have space anyway," he said.
He said expected prices to increase with the announcement of the spring/summer schedule.
"I heard some rumours that there will be a small increase in March or April 1997, with the new schedule," Rehnstrom said.
